source.title: Delegated Classification
source.authors: Eden Saig; Inbal Talgam-Cohen; Nir Rosenfeld

record.tranche_reason: The study applies power-law learning-curve fitting and extrapolation to classification tasks and reports how extrapolation errors affect outcomes. It does not reproduce language-model scaling experiments.
record.gate_note: The study's main theoretical results concern contract design, not scaling laws. It fits power-law curves to classification learning curves for partial-information experiments. Values used only to fit or choose the curve are not recorded as results. Other reported learning-curve and contract-design results do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study's goal is contract design for delegated classifier training. It fits power-law accuracy-versus-training-set-size curves (a - b·n^-c) to small pilot data from LCDB (MNIST; MLP, GBDT and other scikit-learn classifiers). It uses these fits only as a tool to build contracts. Its reported outcomes are delegation performance: attained accuracy, sample-size multiplier, and accuracy loss versus signed extrapolation error. These are measures of its own method. It does not measure language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It also does not assess whether the power-law extrapolation itself is accurate as a test of a scaling law.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right but incomplete. The authors' main conclusions are theoretical. Budget-optimal delegation contracts are min-budget contracts. Binary-action optimal contracts are all-or-nothing, equivalent to the Neyman-Pearson test. Under Concave-MLRP, optimal contracts are threshold contracts. Empirically, threshold contracts built from power-law curves estimated on small pilot data perform well. Contract outcomes are asymmetric in extrapolation error: underestimation degrades gracefully, while overestimation should be avoided because the agent then picks the smallest dataset.
record.recipe_differences: Uses power-law fitting and extrapolation, but studies accuracy versus training-set size for classification tasks and the consequences for delegated contracts, rather than held-out language-model loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Extrapolation error direction; pilot size k; fit range n0; samples per training-set size r.

fits_no_version.finding: Power-law curves fitted to small-n classifier accuracies (MNIST, LCDB) and extrapolated to the incentivized n show signed residuals spanning roughly -0.6 to +0.2 accuracy points across pilot sizes and fit ranges (read from the Fig. 4 right axis). Larger fit range (r=1, larger n0) gives more useful curves than more repetitions per n.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Power-law extrapolation of classifier learning curves (accuracy vs training-set size) from small pilot data has accuracy that depends on fit range more than on repetitions.

fits_no_version.finding: A power law 1 - βn^-γ is fitted to the MNIST MLP accuracy curve, with β̂=1.89 and γ̂=0.33. It is shown visually as a good fit, with no fit statistic.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Classifier accuracy-versus-data learning curves follow a power law.

record.problems: The extrapolation-error results are presented graphically without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The plotted aggregate combines varying pilot sizes, fit ranges, sampling strategies, and repetitions; the text does not identify the classifier for these particular plotted instances.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were reported. Fig. 4's accuracy and effective-sample-size panels describe delegation performance but do not directly measure extrapolation error or the power-law loss relationship.

untested.parts: All: no LM pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no comparison of predicted versus observed loss for LM runs orders of magnitude larger. Classifier accuracy extrapolations serve only as contract inputs.
All: power-law form is assumed for classifier learning curves, not tested.
All: no comparison of exponents or fitting choices as scaling-law results. Fit range (r, n0) is varied only for its effect on contract outcomes.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation for assuming power-law learning curves. The scaling-law material concerns classical classifiers on MNIST, not LMs. No verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Does not directly compare predicted and observed held-out pretraining loss for language-model runs orders of magnitude larger than the fitting runs.
Does not measure compute-optimal parameter and token allocations.
Does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.
Uses power-law fits for classification learning curves but does not test whether the power-law form holds across modalities or training regimes.
Does not measure downstream task performance as a function of pretraining loss or scale.
Does not compare fitted exponents across setups, compute-optimal splits, published scaling laws, or whether curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.operation_detail: Fit power-law accuracy curves using pilot data and extrapolate to larger training-set sizes; assess delegation loss against perfect estimation.

conditions.value: varying k, n0, r, and independent repetitions

rows.measure: Delegation accuracy loss relative to perfect estimation as a function of signed extrapolation error
rows.note: The authors state that accuracy loss degrades gracefully in the underestimation regime. The plot aggregates curve-fitting instances with varying pilot size, fit range, sampling strategy, and repetitions.
rows.check: The measure is the delegation (contract) accuracy loss as a function of extrapolation error. That is the study's own method's sensitivity, not whether power-law fits on small runs predict larger runs. The setting is classifier accuracy versus dataset size, not LM pretraining loss. The subject is the LCDB MNIST learning curves; the classifier is unspecified, likely MLP. It should not be linked to V2.
